evidence.says: Christopher S. Parker: University of Washington faculty from 2006; Chicago political science PhD, 2001; author of Fighting for Democracy (2009) and Change They Can’t Believe In (2013).
Christopher Parker is affiliated with Ghent University; his 2009 works include Tunnel-bypasses and minarets of capitalism and the review Arabic thought in the illiberal age.

basis: The LC books belong to Christopher S. Parker, whose CV identifies his Chicago PhD (2001) and University of Washington appointments. The sole candidate, p-151056, is the Ghent University namesake, distinguished by his contemporaneous institutional affiliation and separate publication record.

evidence.says: LC identifies William George Scott, born 1919, as author of Chester I. Barnard and the guardians of the managerial state (1992).
Smithsonian Libraries lists Chester I. Barnard and the guardians of the managerial state (1992) by William G. Scott.

basis: No source found connects the LC author to the 1973 Wisconsin history dissertation or the 2007 Berkeley history dissertation; management subject matter alone cannot settle those identities. The 1891 Penn doctorate predates his LC-recorded 1919 birth and excludes that candidate.

evidence.says: Page 36 lists Lawrence H. Schwartz, PhD Rutgers University, New Brunswick, as author of Marxism and Culture (1980) and Creating Faulkner’s Reputation (1988).

basis: The MLA profile connects both LC books to a Rutgers PhD, matching the candidate’s doctoral institution. Together with the closely corresponding 1977 dissertation and 1980 book titles, this supports the match by inference; the profile omits the PhD year and dissertation title.

evidence.says: A 1974 review lists John D. Sullivan as coauthor of Unity and Disintegration in International Alliances: Comparative Studies.
In 2024, John Sullivan was a Northwestern history PhD candidate working on Fractious Knowledge: Earthquakes and Engineering in Eighteenth-Century Naples and the Spanish Atlantic.

basis: The review confirms the LC-cited book, and UCLA independently identifies the Northwestern candidate through his dissertation and institution. No source found ties the LC author to either candidate or decisively establishes the identity of the Georgia State candidate relative to the LC author; differences in subject and dissertation year alone are insufficient.
